title: Leptomeningeal metastasis with sturge-weber syndrome-like gyriform calcification on imaging: a case report
author: Yang Liu; Junjun Liu; Chongbo Zhao; Zhiye Wang; Zuonian Zhang; Jie Wei; Yue Zhang
text:
Abstract
Background
Leptomeningeal metastasis (LM) is characterized by the invasion of malignant cells into the leptomeninges of the brain and spinal cord, leading to symptoms like headache, epilepsy, and cognitive impairment. Cases of unilateral extensive gyriform calcification resembling Sturge-Weber syndrome (SWS) on Imaging are extremely rare. We report a case of LM originating from lung adenocarcinoma in which the imaging findings closely similar to those of SWS. The definitive diagnosis of LM was confirmed through histopathological examination.
Case presentation
A 68-year-old right-handed female presented with a 5-month history of rapid cognitive decline, aphasia, irritability, and seizures. Her medical history included radical resection of lung adenocarcinoma 7 years prior. Physical examination revealed no facial hemangioma or other cutaneous stigmata. Brain computed tomography (CT) revealed multiple calcification in the right fronto-temporo-parietal lobe, presenting a typical “tram-track” sign highly reminiscent of SWS. Notably, no calcification were observed on a brain CT performed 18 months earlier. Positron emission tomography-computed tomography (PET-CT) revealed diffuse hypometabolism in the cerebral cortex, while chest CT showed no evidence of lung cancer recurrence. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) cytology identified atypical cells. Eventually, Histopathological examination of a pial biopsy revealed cord-like arrangements of atypical epithelioid cells with associated calcification. Immunohistochemistry was positive for cytokeratin (CK), CK7, thyroid transcription factor-1 (TTF-1), and Napsin-A, with a Ki67 proliferation index of 3%. Genetic analysis identified an epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) L858R mutation, confirming the diagnosis of LM secondary to lung adenocarcinoma. Following one month of osimertinib therapy, the patient exhibited significant improvement in language function.
Conclusions
This case presented diagnostic challenges due to extensive gyriform calcification and the “tram-track” sign, which occasionally resemble SWS. However, the patient’s late onset, absence of prior calcification, and lack of facial hemangioma were atypical for SWS. Furthermore, non-dominant hemisphere calcification did not align with aphasia symptoms. This single-case observation demonstrates that LM may present with radiologically heterogeneous features, and emphasizes the necessity of histopathological confirmation for accurate diagnosis.
Keywords: Leptomeningeal metastasis, Sturge-Weber syndrome, Gyriform calcification, Lung adenocarcinoma
Background
Leptomeningeal metastasis (LM) is a severe oncological complication characterized by the infiltration of malignant cells into the leptomeninges, which disrupts the function of the central nervous system and triggers various neurological symptoms [1]. Common primary tumors include lung cancer, breast cancer, and melanoma, with varied metastatic pathways [2]. Clinical manifestations often include headache, seizures, cognitive decline, cranial nerve palsies, and spinal cord involvement [2].
Sturge-Weber syndrome (SWS) is a rare neurocutaneous disorder caused by somatic mutations in the GNAQ gene, resulting in abnormal vascular development in the skin, brain, and eyes [3]. Typical manifestations include facial port - wine stains, epilepsy, glaucoma, and neurological deficits [4]. Imaging plays a critical role in diagnosis, with brain computed tomography (CT) often revealing characteristic gyriform calcification, known as the “tram-track sign” [4].
Calcification in LM is uncommon [5], and imaging similar to SWS is exceptionally rare. We report a case of LM secondary to lung adenocarcinoma, with imaging features closely resembling SWS, ultimately confirmed by histopathological and immunohistochemical analysis.
Case presentation
A 68-year-old female with established right-handed dominance (Edinburgh Handedness Inventory score + 100) presented with a gradual decline in cognitive function five months prior to admission, characterized by progressively worsening memory, difficulty concentrating, disorientation, frequent involuntary self-talk, and irritability. Despite these deficits, the patient could still engage in basic verbal communication. Over time, her condition deteriorated, resulting in aphasia, loss of independence in activities of daily living (e.g., dressing and grooming), and inability to recognize family members, rendering her fully dependent.
Four days prior to admission, she experienced two acute epileptic episodes. Initial symptoms included involuntary twitching of the left oral commissure, rapidly progressing to left limb convulsions and subsequent generalized tonic-clonic seizures with loss of consciousness. Antiepileptic therapy controlled the seizures and improved her level of consciousness; however, left-sided hemiplegia persisted. She was subsequently admitted to our neurology department for further evaluation and management.
Upon admission, physical examination revealed the patient was somnolent and poorly cooperative, with neck stiffness (three fingerbreadths from chin to sternum). She exhibited aphasia, with left-sided limb strength graded at 2/5 and right-sided strength at 5/5. Neurological assessment demonstrated a positive Babinski sign on the left side, while the right side was negative.
Review of the patient’s medical history revealed curative resection of lung adenocarcinoma seven years prior.
Auxiliary examination results
Brain CT showed multiple gyriform calcification in the right frontal, temporal, and parietal lobes, with some calcification exhibiting a typical “tram-track” appearance (FIGURE 1A-C); Susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) of the same area reveals multiple low signals (considered calcification, FIGURE 1D). Notably, non-contrast MRI sequences - including T1-weighted (FIGURE 1E) and FLAIR imaging (FIGURE 1F) - showed no signal abnormalities in these areas. However, post-contrast T1-weighted imaging revealed distinct enhancement colocalized with the calcified lesions identified on CT (FIGURE 1G). Notably, the patient had presented with complaints of dizziness 18 months prior, and a brain CT scan performed during that evaluation revealed no evidence of calcification (FIGURE 2). Electroencephalogram (EEG) shows diffuse theta and delta waves bilaterally. Brain Positron emission tomography-CT (PET-CT) [Fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG)] indicates reduced whole-brain glucose metabolism. Chest CT shows no signs of lung cancer recurrence. The 18-kDa Translocator Protein (TSPO) PET reveals diffuse, uneven TSPO distribution increase in the cerebral cortex (FIGURE 1H). Blood tests including complete blood count, liver and kidney function, electrolytes, coagulation function, and tumor markers show no significant abnormalities. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis reveals normal routine and biochemical results; paraneoplastic antibody panel and autoimmune encephalitis antibody panel are negative; serum tissue-based assay (TBA) antibody is positive while CSF TBA antibody is negative; CSF cytology identifies atypical cells.
Based on the initial findings, the preliminary clinical diagnosis favored SWS, and levetiracetam was initiated for seizure control. Following treatment, the patient’s level of consciousness improved, left-side limb strength largely returned, and no further epileptic seizures occurred. However, cognitive dysfunction and aphasia persisted without improvement. Critically, the patient’s late-onset presentation, lack of calcifications on prior neuroimaging (18 months earlier), and absence of facial hemangioma were incongruent with a diagnosis of SWS. Furthermore, the observed aphasia anatomically contradicted the right hemispheric lesion in this right-handed individual (a clinical-anatomical dissociation given the expected left hemispheric language dominance). Additionally, bilateral EEG abnormalities indicated diffuse cortical dysfunction discordant with a unilateral structural lesion. Collectively, these findings definitively excluded SWS. Given the diffuse, heterogeneous increase in TSPO distribution on PET and the positive serum TBA antibody, central nervous system immune-inflammatory disease could not be excluded. Methylprednisolone was tried as an anti-inflammatory treatment, but it did not improve the patient’s condition.
Although FDG-PET/CT demonstrated no parenchymal hypermetabolism, the identification of atypical cells in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) provided a pivotal diagnostic clue, suggesting potential neoplastic intracranial involvement. To further clarify the diagnosis, a brain tissue biopsy was performed (FIGURE 3). Biopsy procedure documentation: A small linear incision was created superior to the right auricle. A single cranial burr hole was drilled, followed by dural hemostasis via electrocoagulation. The dura was incised in a cruciform fashion, and the arachnoid membrane was cauterized and incised. Upon accessing the subjacent cortical layer, an abnormal yellowish-white lesion was identified, exhibiting firm consistency, moderate vascularity, and granular calcific deposits. Representative tissue samples were sequentially harvested for intraoperative frozen section and histopathological evaluation. Frozen section analysis demonstrated the presence of atypical cells. A synthetic dural graft was utilized to repair the dural defect, and a titanium cranioplasty plate was implanted to restore the osseous defect. Layered closure of the muscular, subcutaneous, and cutaneous tissues was subsequently completed. Pathological examination revealed epithelioid cells arranged in cords and fissures with atypia, along with calcification (FIGURE 4A). Immunohistochemistry demonstrated positivity for cytokeratin (CK, FIGURE 4B), CK7 (FIGURE 4C), thyroid transcription factor-1 (TTF-1, FIGURE 4D), and Napsin-A (FIGURE 4F), with a Ki67 proliferation index of 3%. Results were negative for Chromogranin A, Synaptophysin, Glial fibrillary acidic protein, Epithelial membrane antigen, Progesterone receptor, and Somatostatin receptor 2a. Genetic testing identified an epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) L858R mutation. Integrating all findings, the final diagnosis was LM from lung adenocarcinoma. After one month of osimertinib treatment, the patient’s aphasia significantly improved, enabling her to articulate short sentences. Follow-up CT (FIGURE 5) at 4-month post-targeted therapy demonstrates stable right fronto-parieto-temporal calcification, unchanged from pretreatment baseline. No new calcification were observed in other neuroanatomical regions.
Discussion and conclusions
The radiological features of LM are highly heterogeneous, typically presenting as meningeal enhancement, hydrocephalus, or parenchymal lesions [6], with calcification being rare [5, 7]. However, this patient’s imaging findings closely resembled SWS, characterized by multiple gyriform calcification in the right frontal, temporal, and parietal lobes, along with a typical “tram-track” appearance. Despite no signs of lung cancer recurrence on chest CT and no high metabolic lesions on PET-CT, the final diagnosis of LM was confirmed through pathological analysis.
In contrast-enhanced CT or MRI, LM manifest as pathological enhancement of the meninges surrounding the brain, cranial nerves, and spinal cord, which may appear as nodular, linear, arcuate, focal, or diffuse patterns of enhancement [1, 2, 6]. In SWS, typical brain CT findings include gyriform calcification and a “tram-track” sign, often accompanied by epilepsy and cognitive decline [4], all of which were present in this patient. However, SWS is a congenital disorder with gyriform calcification typically forming in infancy [3, 8], making it unlikely for them to first appear in the seventh decade of life. Additionally, prior CT imaging revealed no calcification, and the absence of facial hemangiomas further contradicted the diagnosis of SWS. While SWS classically manifests with refractory epilepsy starting in infancy [9], this patient presented with progressive cognitive decline, further distinguishing her clinical course from classic SWS. The calcification in the non-dominant hemisphere could not explain the aphasia or bilateral EEG abnormalities, suggesting more extensive nervous system involvement. The elevated TSPO expression observed in the patient’s cortical regions provides a compelling molecular rationale for prioritizing neuroinflammatory mechanisms in our diagnostic framework. TSPO, a mitochondrial outer membrane protein, regulates cholesterol transport, steroidogenesis, mitochondrial energetics, and apoptosis. In the healthy central nervous system, TSPO exhibits basal expression primarily in microglia–the brain’s resident immune cells [10]. Therefore, elevated TSPO expression directly indicates neuroinflammatory activation [11]. Furthermore, during brain tumorigenesis, rapid tumor cell proliferation, metabolic dysregulation, and tumor microenvironment remodeling stimulate reactive responses in tumor, leading to significant TSPO upregulation [12]. TSPO-PET imaging serves as a vital biomarker for non-invasive visualization of neuroinflammatory processes and cerebral tumor-associated immune activation [10]. Given the positive TBA and negative autoimmune encephalitis antibodies, an unidentified antibody-mediated process was suspected [13]. Thus, we considered central nervous system immune-inflammatory disease as part of the differential diagnosis. However, methylprednisolone treatment did not yield expected improvements. Despite the PET-CT not showing high metabolic activity indicative of epileptogenic tumors, the detection of atypical cells in CSF cytology provided crucial diagnostic clues. Ultimately, brain tissue biopsy confirmed LM.
Calcification in LM is uncommon, observed in only about 1.1% of surgical specimens and 6.6% of autopsy cases [5]. A recent study by Rebella et al. reported a calcification rate of 9.5% among non-irradiated patients with brain metastases [7]. Calcification typically indicates a relatively stable tumor state rather than rapid growth [14]. Given that most leptomeningeal metastatic tumors grow rapidly [14], calcification is rarely seen. However, in cases of slower-growing tumors, such as in the present patient with a low Ki67 index, calcification can occur. The mechanism of calcification is largely unknown but may involve calcification within benign lesions surrounded by the tumor, pathological calcification in areas of tumor necrosis, and calcium deposition due to the secretory function of adenocarcinomas [15].
The management for LM from lung adenocarcinoma primarily includes surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, and targeted therapy [16]. Surgery and radiation are used for local control, while chemotherapy and targeted therapy manage systemic progression [2, 16]. Recent advancements in molecularly targeted therapy have demonstrated that patients with EGFR mutations can benefit from EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) [2, 16, 17]. In this case, genetic testing revealed an EGFR L858R mutation, prompting the selection of the third-generation EGFR-TKI osimertinib. Osimertinib has high blood-brain barrier penetration and effectively inhibits tumor growth in the central nervous system [17]. After one month of treatment, the patient’s language function significantly improved, indicating the effectiveness of osimertinib in this case.
This patient’s imaging findings closely resembled those of SWS, and routine tests failed to provide a definitive diagnosis, posing a diagnostic challenge. Although based on a single observation, this case underscores the heterogeneous radiological manifestations of LM that can occur in rare instances and highlights the critical role of brain tissue biopsy in achieving an accurate diagnosis. Pathological examination not only confirms the diagnosis but also provides crucial molecular information through immunohistochemistry and genetic testing, guiding personalized treatment. Thus, histopathological diagnosis is essential, particularly in cases with atypical imaging.
